== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' was probably born about 1674. This is an uncertain estimate from his entry into an apprenticeship in 1690; his age was not recorded. His birthplace is unknown. Lindsayland in Biggar parish is usable only as an uncertain location inferred from his father's stated residence.

On 7 May 1690 James, son of the deceased James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland, was entered as apprentice to William Brown, a cordiner and tanner in Portsburgh and an Edinburgh burgess. The entry was scored out.<ref name="Apprentice1690">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/edinburgh_apprentices_~_1666_to_1700_~_1929.pdf ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1666–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 37, entry dated 7 May 1690; see also Findmypast, [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FEDINBURGH%2FAPPRENTICES%2F0005159%2F1&tab=this transcript SCOT/EDINBURGH/APPRENTICES/0005159/1], captured 3 September 2026.</ref>

The scoring-out shows that this apprenticeship was cancelled or did not proceed in its entered form. It does not show that James died.

== Research Notes ==
=== Lindsaylands father hypothesis, 20 October 2026 ===

Compared accounts: [[Glasgow-3332|James, proposed father]]; [[Glasgow-4131|James, 1690 apprentice]]; [[Glasgow-1376|James of Whitecastle]]; [[Glasgow-1150|James, Edinburgh weaver]]; [[Glasgow-4114|James, 1696 apprentice]]; [[Glasgow-1086|John, earlier father hypothesis]]; [[Glasgow-3407|Robert, Carnwath hypothesis]].

Watson’s printed Edinburgh apprentice register, p.37 (PDF p.47), names James as son of the deceased James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland. On 7 May 1690 he was entered to William Brown, cordiner in Portsburgh and tanner, burgess; the entry was scored out. The held printed-page image was visually rechecked on 20 October 2026. The entry gives neither the son’s age nor his mother, and cancellation does not establish his death. Grant’s previously inspected Lanark testament index, pp.38/99, records James Glasgow, weaver at Back of Lindsaylands, Biggar parish, on 10 November 1680 (CC14/5/10, testament dative). That is a confirmation/registration date, not an exact death date; its original manuscript remains unread.

Select James Glasgow-3332 as the possible working father of the 1690 apprentice James Glasgow-4131, at 46% subjective confidence. The apprentice’s father is expressly named. His uncommon full name, weaving occupation, specific Lindsayland residence and death before 1690 strongly favour identification with the weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680. Glasgow-3332 is an existing compatible account already compared with that later Biggar weaver; prefer this qualified reuse to creating another same-name father. The overall 46% applies to identifying the named documentary father with that profile, including its unresolved adult identity; it does not express doubt about the explicit father–son wording. The supporting locality and trade are one combined identity argument, not independent proofs.

Glasgow-3332’s independent identity is unresolved. Its estimated 1630/1634 birth and Biggar birthplace do not independently prove the 1680 match, and its inherited John-1086 parent and 1648 Johne child attachments cannot be used circularly to establish it. The alternative 1624 Quothquan-weaver identification is retained; that much earlier decedent is a poor father-generation fit for an ordinary 1690 apprenticeship, but the apprentice has no recorded age. Whitecastle James-1376 remains a compatible possible identity of the later weaver, potentially the same man as James-3332, with no merge. The Edinburgh weaver James-1150 remains a weaker comparison: identifying him with the master active in 1693 would conflict with the father being dead in 1690, but that master’s identity is itself inferred. The 1690 apprentice may still be the 1696 apprentice James-4114 after a cancelled first indenture; the different master and the father’s death must be reconciled before merging them. The 1696 father proposal stays unchanged. No mother, spouse or vital field is transferred or altered. James-3332’s 25% father and Robert-3407’s 23% father hypothesis remain unchanged; the two proposed sons are not proved brothers. This adds one selected profile connection, not a newly discovered son, independent source, or proved pedigree.

Read the 1680 testament for spouse and children, and compare the original 1690/1696 indentures for a repeated identifier or cancellation endorsement. Test the 1648 father and Whitecastle identities separately. A younger apprentice generation is a surviving alternative route for the later Carnwath household, not an automatically inserted father.<ref name="LindsaylandsFatherReview2026">[https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/edinburgh_apprentices_~_1666_to_1700_~_1929.pdf#page=47 Watson, Register of Edinburgh Apprentices, 1666–1700 (1929), printed p.37 / PDF p.47; held page visually rechecked 20 October 2026]; [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments__1595-1800_~_1903.pdf Grant, Commissariot Record of Lanark (1903), pp.38/99; 1680 Lindsaylands weaver; held index account reused]. Printed-page reading rechecked; no new original manuscript inspection.</ref>


=== Apprentice family review —18 October2026 ===

This is the existing1690 apprentice profile,not a person still to create. His father is named James,the deceased Lindsayland weaver; no father profile is selected.

Select the Edinburgh weaver and burgess James [[Glasgow-1150]] as the probable father of the record-defined 1696 apprentice James [[Glasgow-4114]], at 76% subjective confidence. Printed page 37 names the apprentice’s father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Name, occupation, civic status and Edinburgh setting identify a particular established craftsman rather than just a same-name Scottish father. The maintained 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 burgess cross-reference securely establish James-1150 as a weaver and burgess; printed page 72 also records a James Glasgow, weaver and burgess, taking John Paterson as apprentice on 18 October 1693. The maintained burgess-roll review found one matching admission, although an index cannot rule out another man. This makes James-1150 the preferred father-profile match. The child account itself is defined by the 22 April 1696 entry, so no later-life identification is needed for that child.

The 76% is an individual research judgment for the whole father-profile identification, not a measured frequency. The published entry proves a father called James, weaver and burgess; it does not supply his apprenticeship date, wife, home address or age. Another matching craftsman, including a Lindsaylands man who also held burgess rights, remains possible. The circa-1680 child date and circa-1620 father date are estimates, not recorded ages; the nominal sixty-year interval makes late fatherhood relevant but is not a contradiction. James’s 1641 apprenticeship supplies no exact birth year. The younger James’s mother remains unknown: neither Bessie Whyte nor Agnes Duncan is transferred merely because she married the proposed father. The father’s existing probable Robert ancestry and all other family grades remain unchanged.

The earlier claim that the 1690 and 1696 apprentices must be different men is withdrawn. The 1690 entry explicitly calls its Lindsayland weaver father deceased and says that the apprenticeship was scored out. The 1696 entry omits a death qualification; silence does not prove that father alive. A cancelled cordiner apprenticeship followed by an apothecary apprenticeship six years later is compatible with one man, although not established. The matching apprentice/father names and father’s weaving trade support testing that possibility; burgess status is given only for the 1696 father and the two masters differ. Keep the two existing profiles distinct pending an identifier; do not create them again. If they prove to be one child, the selected James-1150 father would need reconsideration because the 1690 father was dead whereas the Edinburgh master appears in 1693. This alternative limits the father assessment rather than being erased.

James [[Glasgow-1376]] is not excluded from the 1696 apprentice merely because his former 1657 birth was a misread parent role. Removing that false date supplies no identity conflict. His Whitecastle adult occurrence in 1672 makes a 1696 first apprenticeship less ordinary, and no trade or residence bridge identifies him; retain him as a weaker compatible comparison. The proposed father of Whitecastle James is unchanged. Other Edinburgh James households remain comparisons, without unproved mergers, sibling transfers or replacement birth dates.

This materialises a father already favoured in the apprentice’s live biography, whose structured Father field is still zero; it is a genuinely outstanding new father attachment, not a confidence correction to an attached father. Both apprentices were already created on WikiTree. Their record-only creation suggestions are retired in favour of those exact profiles. No live edit, new WikiTree person or new manuscript discovery is claimed. The inspected source is Watson’s 1929 printed register, not the original city register; earlier citations incorrectly named Henry Paton as editor.

Check the original indentures for cancellation, endorsement or a repeated identifier; compare the 1690 and 1696 apprentices before merging them. Seek the weaver’s testament or incorporation family entry for wife and sons. The 1696 master reads Wm. Adam, not the Findmypast transcript’s Adamson. A score-out does not establish a death.

Earlier statements asserting that the two apprentices must be different people,or excluding a profile only because a field or extra corroboration is missing,are retained below as historical assessments and are superseded by this review.


The father is probably the James Glasgow, weaver at Back of Lindsaylands, whose testament was registered in the Lanark Commissary Court on 10 November 1680.<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments_1595-1800_~_1903.pdf ''The Commissariot Record of Lanark: Register of Testaments, 1595–1800''] (Scottish Record Society, 1903), printed p. 38.</ref> The exact name, occupation, distinctive locality and prior death make that documentary identity strong, but the testament must be inspected before attaching a profile or naming the apprentice's mother.

This James is not the apprentice entered in 1696: the 1690 father was already dead, whereas the 1696 father was a living weaver and burgess. [[Glasgow-3076|James Glasgow]], born at Edinburgh in 1661, is excluded because his profile supplies no Lindsayland or correct-father bridge and he would have been unusually old for this entry.
